title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description:
# Search in Rotated Sorted Array

A strictly increasing array of unique integers may be rotated by moving a suffix to the front. For example, `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` may become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`.

Given the possibly rotated array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` if it appears in `nums`; otherwise return `-1`.

Use `O(log n)` time, where `n` is the array length.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target = 0

**Output:** 4

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target = 3

**Output:** -1

## Example 3

**Input:** nums = [1], target = 0

**Output:** -1

## Constraints

* `1 <= nums.length <= 5000`
* `-10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000`
* All values in `nums` are unique.
* `nums` is an ascending sorted array that may be rotated.
* `-10000 <= target <= 10000`

tests.description: Target found in the rotated right segment
Target absent from a rotated array
Target immediately before the rotation drop
Unrotated array with target in the middle
Unrotated array with missing target above range
Rotated array with target in the middle of the right segment
Rotated array with target at the first element
Rotated array with target at the last element
Rotation crossing from positive to negative values
Missing target below the negative rotated segment

solutions.name: One-Pass Rotated Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Run binary search directly on the rotated array. At each step, first test `nums[mid]`. Then decide whether the left half `[left, mid]` or the right half `[mid, right]` is sorted, and keep the half whose value range can contain `target`.

## Key Insight

With unique values, at least one half of any interval is sorted. That sorted half gives a normal binary-search range test, so each iteration safely discards half of the remaining candidates.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Find Pivot Then Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

First find the index of the minimum value using the same pivot search as the previous problem. The pivot splits the array into two sorted ranges. Choose the range whose boundary values can contain `target`, then run ordinary binary search inside that physical range.

## Key Insight

This separates the rotation problem from the lookup problem. Once the pivot is known, both sides are standard sorted arrays, so the second phase is ordinary binary search.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Virtual Sorted Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Find the pivot, then binary search virtual indices `0..n-1` as if the array had been rotated back into sorted order. A virtual index `mid` maps to the real array index `(pivot + mid) % n`.

## Key Insight

The values encountered through the virtual index order are sorted. This keeps the second phase as one ordinary binary search and teaches index remapping as an alternative to choosing a physical half.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Recursive Rotated Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the one-pass rotated binary-search rule recursively. Each call checks the midpoint, identifies the sorted half, and recurses only into the half whose value range can still contain the target.

## Key Insight

The recursive form exposes the divide-and-conquer invariant: every call receives a contiguous interval that may contain the answer. The sorted-half test proves which recursive branch is still possible.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)
